web_blocks.text: The supplied fundamentals-only extract extends the financial lens from FY23–FY26 to twelve annual observations from March 2015 through March 2026. It is a secondary structured dataset sourced to Screener, not a primary filing; its rows are rounded and the JSON does not state a unit. FY25 and FY26 sales values of 557 and 711 align with the audited annual report’s ₹556.98 crore and ₹711.07 crore, so longer-period sales, operating profit and PAT are discussed as approximate ₹ crore only after that cross-check. The annual report remains the source of record for FY25/FY26 where available. [12][1]

web_blocks.caption: Audited standalone financial trajectory, ₹ crore except EPS (₹). FY23–FY26 annual report series; EPS reflects the disclosed share subdivision restatement. [1][2]

web_blocks.text: The pattern is not a straight line. Revenue was almost flat between FY23 and FY24, then rose sharply in FY25 and FY26 as capacity and demand expanded. FY25 was the profit peak in this four-year series: the company attributes unusually strong realizations, particularly in Q3, to a temporary demand–supply gap. FY26 revenue set a new high, but operating EBITDA fell from ₹128.9 crore to ₹112.1 crore and PAT from ₹88.1 crore to ₹70.1 crore as input costs normalized upward and depreciation increased after recent capacity additions. Revenue growth, margin movement and profit therefore diverged. [1][2][3]

web_blocks.caption: Audited cash conversion and investment, ₹ crore; annual periods are matched. [1]
rows: Cash purchase of property, plant and equipment

web_blocks.text: Cash conversion improved in absolute terms in FY26, but operating cash flow remained below PAT: approximately 62% of PAT in FY26 versus 37% in FY25, calculated from the audited figures. Working capital absorbed ₹52.84 crore in FY26 after absorbing ₹69.54 crore in FY25; tax payments were a further outflow. PPE cash expenditure was ₹82.45 crore in FY26, and net investing cash flow was more negative because investing activity also includes movements in investments. This is why CFO, capex and total investing cash flow should not be treated as interchangeable. [1]

At March 2026, total equity was ₹373.2 crore, current borrowings ₹92.8 crore, cash and cash equivalents ₹21.1 crore, current investments ₹17.0 crore and reported net debt ₹46.6 crore; there were no non-current borrowings at that date. The post-year-end QIP raised ₹250 crore in June 2026, followed by a roughly ₹100-crore preferential issue in September, including promoter participation. By September 2026, the company reported total equity of ₹736.8 crore, borrowings of ₹135.6 crore across current and non-current classifications, cash of ₹99.1 crore and current investments of ₹58.4 crore; its investor presentation characterized net debt as negative. These capital raises strengthened the balance sheet but also expanded the equity base. [1][4][6]

Per-share outcomes should be separated from operating outcomes. FY25 and FY26 EPS fell from ₹44.18 to ₹35.16 alongside lower PAT; the annual report notes the weighted-average share count was unchanged between those two years after share subdivision. In H1 FY27, the QIP and preferential issuance increased share capital, and the reported weighted-average EPS was ₹17.35 versus ₹18.31 for H1 FY26 while PAT was approximately level at ₹35.9 crore versus ₹36.5 crore. The exact contribution from operations, timing and dilution is therefore not captured by revenue growth alone. [1][4]

web_blocks.title: Secondary-history and product-mix boundary
paragraphs: The supplied Screener extract adds twelve annual observations from Mar 2015 to Mar 2026, useful for cycle analysis but rounded and secondary. The company’s audited FY25/FY26 statements are the primary reconciliation points; earlier raw rows should not be labeled audited. The annual report still discloses one operating segment and no product-level revenue or profit split. [12][1]

web_blocks.caption: Calculated margins and annual revenue growth based on the reported FY23–FY26 financial series; percentages are arithmetic derived from company-reported figures. [1][2]

web_blocks.text: The margin series makes the financial cycle more legible. FY24 revenue barely advanced from FY23, while gross margin improved and operating EBITDA margin softened slightly. FY25 then combined strong sales growth with a temporary realization benefit, lifting gross, EBITDA and PAT margins to the four-year highs. FY26 delivered another substantial increase in revenue, but gross margin fell by roughly 7.7 percentage points and EBITDA margin by about 7.4 points from FY25; PAT margin declined by about 6 points. These are calculated differences from reported percentages. They should not be described as a deterioration in physical scale: FY26 was also reported as the highest year for production and revenue. [1][2][3]

web_blocks.text: The H1 FY27 balance-sheet expansion needs a capital-structure lens. The QIP and preferential issue together raised about ₹350 crore, and the filing shows total equity rising from ₹373.2 crore at March to ₹736.8 crore at September. Share capital moved from ₹10.0 crore to ₹10.8 crore; the Q2 presentation says the weighted-average EPS calculation includes shares issued in the QIP and preferential allotment. The new equity gives the projects funding flexibility, but per-share earnings should not be compared without recognizing the larger share base. At the same time, September borrowings include ₹66.1 crore non-current and ₹69.5 crore current debt, so the balance sheet should be read as a full set of cash, investments, borrowings and equity—not as a single debt figure. [1][4]

Working capital was a real swing factor in both audited years and the latest half. In FY25, working-capital changes used ₹69.54 crore; in FY26, they used ₹52.84 crore, while the reported cycle improved eight days to 91. In H1 FY27, the company increased fluorspar stock to approximately six to seven months of cover as a precaution against longer lead times, compared with a normal three to four months. Management said creditors rose alongside the inventory buffer and that about 70% of the receivable increase was collected in October. These explanations are management-reported; subsequent statements would be needed to confirm that the temporary inventory and receivable bulge normalized. [1][2][4][6]

The new structured history fills an important horizon gap, but it does not remove source limitations. It provides twelve annual columns from Mar 2015 to Mar 2026 and a September 2026 balance-sheet update; the extract is secondary, rounded, and not a substitute for audited statements. Use it to identify cycles and long-run patterns, then use primary annual reports for precise FY25/FY26 results. Its ratios also have their own calculation conventions, which are not fully specified in the extract. [12][1][4]

For operating cash conversion, the central FY26 question is not whether cash was positive, but why it lagged accounting profit during a major build-out. The indirect cash-flow statement starts from profit before tax and comprehensive income, adds depreciation and non-cash/financial adjustments, then shows working-capital absorption and tax payments. Operating cash flow rose from ₹32.84 crore in FY25 to ₹43.40 crore in FY26, but remained below PAT in both years. PPE cash purchases were ₹97.03 crore and ₹82.45 crore respectively; the FY26 investing outflow also included investment movements. Financing cash flow was positive as borrowings funded part of the capacity program. That is an expansion-cycle cash pattern, not evidence that all earnings converted to distributable cash. [1]

web_blocks.title: Separate the financial questions
paragraphs: Revenue growth measures scale; EBITDA margin captures operating conversion before depreciation and finance costs; PAT includes depreciation, financing and tax; EPS also reflects the share count; CFO includes working-capital and tax cash movements; capital raises fund the balance sheet; commissioning and product ramp determine whether new assets earn. No one metric answers all of them. [1][4]

web_blocks.text: The long record separates into distinct operating regimes. In the secondary table, sales move from about 120 in FY15 to 222 in FY19, then contract to 165 in FY20 and 148 in FY21. Operating profit falls from 53 in FY19 to 27 in FY20, while operating margin moves from 24% to 16%; the table records PAT declining from 36 to 17. Sales then rise to 320 in FY22 and 375 in FY23, remain nearly flat at 378 in FY24, and accelerate to 557 and 711 in FY25/FY26. Operating profit reaches 131 in FY25 before easing to 114 in FY26, and PAT moves from 88 to 70. The supplied retrospective profile separately describes an earlier severe downturn linked to the 2007 crisis and Chinese competition, but it does not provide audited figures for that episode. [12][9][1]

web_blocks.text: The margins demonstrate why sales alone do not describe the cycle. Screener’s rounded operating-margin series is 7–13% through FY15–FY18, 24% in FY19, 16% in FY20, 22–24% in FY21–FY22, 20% and 19% in FY23–FY24, 24% in FY25 and 16% in FY26. These are secondary rows, not audited margins. The FY25 peak and FY26 normalization are consistent with the company’s account of exceptional realizations in FY25 followed by higher input costs and depreciation in FY26. The direction is supported by the audited annual report, while the exact FY25/FY26 operating-margin definition must be reconciled to the audited P&L rather than copied blindly from the rounded row. [12][1][3]

web_blocks.text: Capital structure and reinvestment show a long transition. The secondary balance sheet records borrowings of 69 in FY15, declining to zero by FY20 and remaining at zero through FY24; borrowings return at 41 in FY25 and 93 in FY26, with 136 shown at September 2026. The annual report confirms FY26 current borrowings of ₹92.81 crore and no non-current borrowings at year-end; the H1 FY27 filing reports term and current borrowings after the equity raises. The asset side moves with the build-out: fixed assets rise from 61 in FY24 to 168 in FY25 and 212 in FY26, while CWIP is 29, 8 and 29 respectively, then 153 at September 2026. These rounded secondary rows describe expansion, not the profitability of each project. [12][1][4]

web_blocks.text: Cash generation was positive in every annual CFO row of the supplied table, but reinvestment changed the free-cash pattern. Screener’s FCF row is positive from FY15 through FY23, turns slightly negative in FY24, and reaches approximately negative 64 in FY25 and negative 39 in FY26. The FY25/FY26 values are close to audited CFO less PPE cash purchases, so the expansion-cycle interpretation is supported for those two years. Do not call all FCF figures audited: the earlier annual rows have not been cross-checked to their primary cash-flow statements here. The extract’s cash-conversion ratio is also ambiguous: its row label says “CFO/EBITDA,” but its description says CFO before tax divided by operating profit. Treat that sequence as directional rather than a consistently defined audited ratio. [12][1]

Working-capital days reveal another cycle hidden by group-level revenue. In the secondary series, debtor days fall from 52 in FY15 to 28 in FY22, then rise to 65 in FY25 before easing to 57 in FY26. Inventory days vary from 66 in FY17 to 134 in FY21, fall to 89 in FY23, rise to 112 in FY25 and decline to 79 in FY26. Payable days drop from 142 in FY21 to 21 in FY26. The dataset’s cash-conversion-cycle row consequently rises from 31 days in FY21 to 129 in FY25 and 115 in FY26. The annual report separately gives its working-capital cycle as 99 days in FY25 and 91 in FY26; these are differently defined series and should not be forced into a single trend. [12][1]

The secondary ROCE row is also volatile: it records 4% in FY15, reaches 78% in FY19, falls to 35% in FY21, rises to 67% in FY22, then moves through 48%, 33%, 42% and 24% in FY23–FY26. The FY25/FY26 figures do not match the annual report’s 33.67% and 20.19%. This may reflect formula or denominator differences, but the supplied extract does not document enough to reconcile the full history. Use the series to flag that reported returns have not been smooth; use audited company ratios for the last two years and avoid combining the two definitions. [12][1]

Dilution must be distinguished from operating performance. The secondary balance sheet rounds equity capital to 10 through Mar 2026 and 11 at Sep 2026, while the H1 filing reports share capital rising from ₹10.0 crore to ₹10.8 crore after the QIP and preferential issue. FY25/FY26 weighted-average shares were unchanged after the disclosed subdivision, and audited EPS declined from ₹44.18 to ₹35.16 with lower PAT. H1 FY27 EPS was ₹17.35 versus ₹18.31, with near-flat PAT and new shares included in the weighted average. The extract’s historical EPS is rounded and differs slightly from audited restated figures for some years; use it directionally and prefer audited numbers for precise comparisons. [12][1][4]

web_blocks.title: Forensic conclusion: a longer cycle, with two source boundaries
paragraphs: The 2015–2026 secondary history supports a real decade-scale review of sales, profitability, reinvestment, cash conversion and working-capital volatility. It is rounded and secondary, so FY25/FY26 must be reconciled to audited statements and earlier raw values must not be described as audited. Separately, the company reports one operating segment and does not disclose product-level revenue or profit mix. [12][1]

book_paragraphs: Read TANFAC’s four-year financial record as a cycle plus an investment program. The top line accelerated from FY25, but the FY25 profit peak did not repeat in FY26. Higher sulphur costs and new-asset depreciation compressed profitability even as production and revenue reached records. That distinction matters: a growing sales base can coexist with lower earnings when spreads normalize and the depreciation charge catches up with commissioned plant. The secondary extract now supplies twelve annual observations from Mar 2015 to Mar 2026, enough to examine multiple cycles; it is rounded and not audited, so use it for pattern recognition and reconcile FY25/FY26 to primary filings. [12][1] [1][2][3]

Then follow earnings into cash and capital. FY26 operating cash flow of ₹43.40 crore was below PAT of ₹70.14 crore, while PPE cash purchases were ₹82.45 crore. Working capital consumed cash, and the balance sheet carried net debt at year-end before the subsequent equity raises. The June QIP and September preferential issue strengthened equity and funded expansion, while increasing the share base. In your analysis, keep operating growth, margins, EPS, capital raising, cash conversion and product ramp in separate columns; each answers a different question. [1][4][6]

Your financial review should begin with the shape, not a single CAGR. The disclosed FY23–FY26 series shows a flat revenue transition into FY24, a sharp rise in FY25, and further growth in FY26. The margin sequence peaks in FY25 and then compresses in FY26. Management links FY25’s unusually favorable realization to a temporary supply-demand gap; FY26 adds raw-material pressure and higher depreciation from newly commissioned assets. The result is a clear separation between physical expansion and earnings conversion. Revenue growth is real in the reported data, but it did not preserve FY25 profitability. [1][2][3]

Next, follow cash through the audited statements. FY26 operating cash flow of ₹43.40 crore did not match the ₹70.14 crore PAT; working capital absorbed ₹52.84 crore and direct taxes used cash. PPE purchases were ₹82.45 crore, while net investing outflow was larger because investments also moved. FY25 had still lower CFO relative to PAT and higher PPE purchases. If you looked only at profit, you would miss how inventory, receivables, taxes and construction compete for funds. If you looked only at total investing cash flow, you might confuse securities transactions with plant spending. [1]

The balance sheet changed materially after the fiscal year. At March 2026, TANFAC reported ₹46.6 crore net debt, current borrowings of ₹92.8 crore, cash and equivalents of ₹21.1 crore, and equity of ₹373.2 crore. It then raised approximately ₹250 crore in a QIP and roughly ₹100 crore in a preferential issue during H1 FY27. By September, equity was ₹736.8 crore, cash ₹99.1 crore and borrowings were split between current and non-current classifications. The strengthened funding base is relevant to project execution, while the larger share count changes the per-share lens. Do not treat the equity raise as operating profit or the post-raise balance sheet as the FY26 year-end position. [1][4]

Per-share analysis deserves its own row. FY25 EPS of ₹44.18 fell to ₹35.16 in FY26 as PAT declined; the annual report says the weighted-average share count was unchanged across those two years after the split adjustment. In H1 FY27, the reported EPS was ₹17.35 versus ₹18.31, while PAT was roughly flat, and new shares from the two raises were included in weighted-average shares. Those comparisons separate the earnings numerator from the share denominator. They do not establish future dilution or operating quality on their own; they show why sales, profits and per-share results should not be blended. [1][4]

The longer secondary record now lets you compare FY15–FY26, including the FY19 peak, FY20–FY21 contraction, FY22 step-up, FY23–FY24 plateau, and FY25–FY26 expansion with margin normalization. It remains a structured secondary series rather than a decade of audited annual reports; the retrospective downturn account adds qualitative context, not missing audited values. The resulting conclusion is stronger but still bounded: the company has moved through different sales, margin, debt and cash-conversion regimes, while the precise pre-FY23 statement details and product-level economics remain unavailable in primary form. [12][1][2][9]

You can make the cash-quality discussion more exact by following the FY26 indirect-method reconciliation. The audited statement starts with profit before tax and comprehensive income, adds depreciation and other non-cash or investment-related adjustments, and reaches operating profit before working-capital changes of ₹117.24 crore. Receivables, inventory, payables and provisions then consume ₹52.84 crore; net taxes paid consume another ₹21.00 crore, leaving ₹43.40 crore of operating cash. The company simultaneously spent ₹82.45 crore on property, plant and equipment, with that line including CWIP movements, advances and capital creditors. This is a transparent accounting bridge, not an estimate of maintenance capex or future free cash flow. [1]

Balance-sheet dates must also stay aligned. The March net-debt figure belongs to the pre-QIP fiscal year-end. The June QIP and September preferential issue materially increased equity; by September, borrowings were divided between current and non-current categories and cash and investments were higher. The company described its H1 net-debt position as negative, but a reader should not subtract selected balance-sheet categories using an unstated definition. Use the company’s stated description and the date-specific components, and leave the calculation method explicit if a later analysis elects to derive a net-cash figure. [1][2][4]

Finally, recognize the denominator effect in per-share data. FY26 EPS fell with PAT from the FY25 peak, while the annual report says the weighted-average share count was unchanged in those fiscal years after the share subdivision. H1 FY27 brought new equity issuances and a larger share capital; its weighted-average EPS was lower year on year while PAT was approximately flat. This is neither a reason to ignore the funding nor a reason to attribute the entire EPS change to operations. Earnings per share contains both the earnings numerator and the share denominator. Keep each visible so that future project returns can be assessed on a per-share basis when the operating record matures. [1][4]

Be precise about what the expanded history can answer. The Mar 2015–Mar 2026 secondary tables provide annual sales, operating profit, PAT, balance-sheet, cash-flow and ratio rows; the FY25/FY26 audited statements allow a useful check on rounding and line definitions. The long view reveals contractions, rebounds and margin variation that the recent four-year series alone obscured. It still does not provide audited primary statements for every year or explain every movement. Use the structured series to ask better cycle questions, and reserve precise audited claims for the years that can be reconciled. [12][1][2]

In a forensic review, the secondary decade-scale history is useful precisely because it exposes variation: margins peak and recede, borrowing falls and later returns, and free cash flow turns negative during the latest investment phase. But a rounded ratio series is not a normalized through-cycle rate. The audited FY25/FY26 checks anchor the recent period; the company’s one-segment disclosure still prevents product-level attribution. State both strengths and limits so that the longer horizon improves the analysis without creating false precision. [12][1][2]

Finally, do not label every balance-sheet change as debt reduction or every capital raise as operational improvement. At FY26 year-end, the company had recorded borrowings and net debt while investing in capacity; after year-end, the QIP and preferential issue changed equity, cash and the funding profile. The September balance sheet also records term and current borrowings. A consistent comparison requires date alignment and a clear definition of net debt. Likewise, cash generated from operations is not free cash flow after project spending, and PAT is not cash available for distribution. Keep those measures distinct in the final forensic narrative. [1][4]

You can now see a much fuller operating cycle. Sales rise from about 120 in FY15 to 222 by FY19, contract to 165 and 148 over FY20–FY21, then step to 320 in FY22. The next two years are nearly flat at 375 and 378; FY25 and FY26 then reach 557 and 711. The profit path is less smooth than the sales path: the secondary table records PAT of negative 5 in FY15, 36 in FY19, 17 in FY20–FY21, 53 in FY22, 52–56 in FY23–FY24, 88 in FY25 and 70 in FY26. The message is not a uniform compounder curve; it is a business with contraction, recovery, a plateau, and a capacity-linked acceleration. [12][1]

You should read the operating-profit row with a definition check beside it. In FY25 and FY26, Screener’s rounded “Operating Profit” of 131 and 114 is closer to audited PBDIT of 131.82 and 114.41 crore than to TANFAC’s reported operating EBITDA of 128.86 and 112.06 crore. The difference is broadly the other-income component. That cross-check prevents a false conclusion that the source values exactly reproduce the company’s EBITDA series. For earlier years there is no matched audited series in this task, so retain the source label and mark the data as secondary. [12][1]

Cash quality changes with the investment phase. The structured table records positive CFO throughout, but its FCF row shifts from positive values through FY23 to negative 2 in FY24, negative 64 in FY25 and negative 39 in FY26. The last two figures reconcile closely to audited operating cash less cash PPE purchases. The decade-scale pattern therefore shows that positive operating cash can coexist with negative post-investment cash during capacity expansion. Do not present Screener’s earlier FCF entries as audited, and do not call its cash-conversion ratio definitive while the label and formula description differ. [12][1]

The working-capital data give you a more granular question than a single company-reported cycle. Receivables stretch in FY23–FY25 before easing in FY26; inventory days fluctuate sharply, and payable days shorten by FY26. The secondary cash-conversion-cycle row remains elevated at 115 days in FY26, while the annual report gives a 91-day working-capital cycle. That is not a reason to choose whichever number supports a preferred story. It is a reason to keep the definitions distinct, use the source’s own labels, and explain that the secondary extract does not state enough methodology to bridge them. [12][1]

Capital allocation also looks different over twelve observations. Borrowings decline from 69 in FY15 to zero by FY20, remain at zero through FY24, and reappear at 41 and 93 in FY25 and FY26 as fixed assets and construction work increase. The September 2026 balance sheet shows much higher CWIP, while QIP and preferential equity also enlarge the funding base and share count. This is a debt-and-reinvestment cycle, not simply a return to permanent leverage: distinguish the earlier deleveraging period, the recent funded capex, and the post-raise capital structure. The exact FY25/FY26 balance-sheet figures should remain anchored to audited filings. [12][1][4]

ROCE in the secondary data is notably volatile, including unusually high points in FY19 and FY22 and a decline by FY26. The annual report’s FY25/FY26 return measures are lower than the corresponding secondary values, confirming that formula differences matter. Ratios depend on the numerator, average versus closing capital and inclusion of cash or other assets; the provided Screener extract does not document those choices. You can use the series to observe volatility and identify periods for investigation, but not to calculate a single normalized return rate without consistent definitions and primary statement data. [12][1]

Finally, the new series improves the long-cycle account without changing the evidence standard. You now have enough observations to describe sales and profit regimes, balance-sheet de-leveraging and renewed borrowing, investment-led negative FCF, working-capital variation and return-ratio volatility. You do not have audited full statements for every year, and you still lack product-level revenue and profit disclosures. Your synthesis should therefore be more historically informed, not more certain than the source allows. Use rounded rows to locate the questions; use audited reports to answer them where available. [12][1]

book_callouts.title: Reflection — earnings quality over a cycle
book_callouts.text: What changed between revenue, EBITDA, PAT, EPS and CFO across FY25–FY27? Which differences reflect operating spreads, which reflect depreciation and working capital, and which reflect new shares? If the permitted record cannot answer a ten-year question, leave it explicitly unanswered. [1][2][4]
